extracted.intended_audience: students, economists, policymakers, and historians studying banking, monetary policy, and the effects of paper money
extracted.subtask_description: Normative and descriptive guidance on prudent banking operations, the issuance and denomination of bank notes, detection of fictitious bills, and the broader economic and public-policy effects of paper money. Focused on how banks should behave and how paper circulation interacts with specie, trade, and public credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real and circulating bills of exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks and bankers ought to distinguish between a real bill drawn by a real creditor upon a real debtor, and a bill for which there was properly no real creditor but the bank which discounted it, nor any real debtor but the projector who made use of the money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives the example of adventurers who draw and redraw bills to raise money; when these bills are repeatedly discounted and replaced by larger bills, the advances are effectively fictitious. Banks discounting such bills advance capital that is not really returned to them. Detection is difficult when drawers discount with different bankers or circulate through a wide circle of projectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid discounting fictitious/redrawn bills that create artificial circulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Discounting bills that are merely part of a circular chain of redrawings (i.e., raising money by circulation rather than by real capital) is essentially lending against nothing and empties bank coffers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such operations may let projectors carry on longer but only deepen eventual ruin; they are costly (commissions and interest accumulate) and result in paper that returns upon banks and must be exchanged for specie or funded by drawing on other financial centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise prudent restraint in discounting to protect bank and public credit
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks must sometimes refuse further discounts, even though that refusal may bankrupt borrowers, because continued discounting would endanger the bank and public credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a banker finds he has discounted too much, he may need to withdraw gradually—making greater difficulties about discounting day by day—to force projectors to other resources. This gradual withdrawal is prudent to avoid immediate ruin of bank and borrowers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not indiscriminately discount without distinguishing bill quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A bank that discounts without distinguishing between real and circulating bills (i.e., discounts all alike) risks excessive issue of bank notes and long-run aggravation of distress rather than relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The example of a new Scottish bank that discounted all bills equally led to over-issuance, empty coffers, and ultimately required drawing bills on London; its temporary relief to projectors aggravated the country's distress in the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit issuance of bank notes to what the circulation can absorb
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing paper beyond what the country's circulation can absorb leads to notes returning upon the issuing bank to be exchanged for gold and silver, emptying its coffers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Much of the paper issued for large projects was over and above the value of specie that would have circulated; such over-issuance causes continual demands for redemption or borrowing to pay off returning notes, forcing banks to draw on other financial centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain sufficient specie reserves; avoid relying on drawing bills abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks should keep coffers adequately filled and should not depend on the ruinous expedient of drawing bills on other places (e.g., London) to fund continual redemptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeatedly drawing bills on London and paying them by other draughts on the same place (with accumulated interest and commission) is compared to refilling a leaking pond by carrying water miles with buckets — it is costly and unsustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict small-denomination banknotes to prevent fragile banking and specie exile
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing notes in very small sums (e.g., shillings, sixpences, or twenty shillings) extends paper into retail circulation, tends to banish gold and silver, and encourages many small, fragile bankers whose frequent bankruptcies harm poor note-holders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where no bank notes are circulated under £10 (as in London), paper confines itself to dealers' circulation and gold/silver remain plentiful. The author suggests it may be better that no notes be issued under £5 so paper mainly serves dealers, reducing risk to consumers and specie exile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine paper money chiefly to circulation between dealers when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Paper money confined to wholesale circulation (dealer-to-dealer) allows banks to assist commerce without displacing specie in retail transactions; when paper extends to dealer-consumer circulation, specie is banished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-denomination notes circulate more slowly in retail and thus tend not to displace small-change specie. Banking functions (discounting real bills, lending on cash-accounts) can still relieve dealers of holding dead stock even if paper is limited to dealers' circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use banking to convert 'dead stock' into active productive stock
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicious banking operations increase industry by enabling dealers to convert the part of their capital kept as ready money (dead stock) into active productive stock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting paper for a portion of specie permits capital formerly idle as ready money to be used for materials, tools, subsistence — thereby increasing annual produce. Yet this benefit comes with increased exposure to accidents from mismanagement of paper money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against excessive multiplication of paper money for national security and stability
rubrics_metrics.description: A country whose circulation is largely paper suffers greater confusion if an enemy seizes capital supporting paper credit; excessive paper makes wartime recovery far more difficult than circulating specie would.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because taxes and government payments are usually in paper, loss of the treasure that supports its credit could prevent a prince from paying troops or supplying magazines; thus governments should guard against both ruinous multiplication and even large expansion of paper money.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banks should be judicious in choice of debtors; avoid funding speculative projectors
rubrics_metrics.description: A bank that lends widely to many unknown borrowers is less likely to choose prudent debtors than private lenders who know their borrowers; banks risk transferring capital to chimerical projectors and unprofitable undertakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bank that lends to hundreds of people (many unknown) will likely finance extravagant undertakings that won't repay their costs; private lenders' sober choices yield more solid, profitable projects and greater sustained employment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banknotes must be payable on demand and readily paid to be equivalent to specie
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper money consisting in bank notes issued by people of undoubted credit and payable on demand, and actually readily paid as presented, is equal in value to gold and silver money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If banknotes are thus reliably redeemable, whatever is bought or sold for such paper will be as cheap as if bought for gold or silver; redeemability is the key attribute making paper equivalent to specie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that increasing paper money raises money prices of commodities
rubrics_metrics.description: An increase of paper money, by augmenting quantity and diminishing value of the whole currency, necessarily augments the money price of commodities (i.e., causes inflation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows from the mechanics of currency quantity and value — expanding paper beyond productive capacity or specie backing devalues the currency and raises nominal prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directors should not allow shareholders to borrow against unpaid subscriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing proprietors to borrow upon cash-accounts what they have not yet paid in on subsequent instalments is imprudent and only shuffles funds between coffers without really increasing reserves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the cited bank, many proprietors paid only the first instalment and then borrowed those sums back; such practices meant coffers were never truly filled, leaving the bank vulnerable to rapid depletion and the need to draw on London.

rubrics_metrics.name: Banks serving public/state functions may overstock circulation; weigh public duty vs. monetary stability
rubrics_metrics.description: A national bank acting as an engine of state (receiving/paying annuities, circulating exchequer bills, advancing taxes) may be obliged, without fault of directors, to overstock the circulation with paper money, with attendant risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Bank of England, by supporting public credit and advancing large sums, sometimes had to augment circulation; such actions have trade-offs: supporting public credit vs. risking over-issuance and its effects on economy and specie availability.
